script:
Somewhere around eleven tonight, a version of you is going to make a promise. It might be a small one. Tomorrow you'll get up when the alarm goes off. Tomorrow you'll leave the phone on the other side of the room. Tomorrow you'll finally send the message you've been rewriting in your head for a month. And while that version of you is making the promise, it will feel completely real. You'll mean every word of it. You might even feel a little lighter, the way people do when they've finally decided something.

Then six o'clock comes. A different version of you opens one eye, does some very fast arithmetic involving warmth, sleep, and how much the day actually matters, and quietly cancels the whole arrangement.

Same body. Same brain. Same name on the same door. And yet two completely different governments, and the second one always seems to hold the real power.

I want to begin there, because the sentence we're going to spend this time with sounds so clean that it's easy to miss the odd thing hiding inside it. Master yourself, and you will master your life. To master yourself, there has to be a master, and there has to be someone being mastered. Two parties, living in one person. If you have ever broken a promise you made to yourself, you already know those two parties exist, and you already know they don't always agree about who is in charge.

So before we talk about discipline, or routines, or any of the advice that usually travels with this idea, there's a more basic question that almost nobody stops to ask. When you say you want to master yourself, who, exactly, is doing the mastering? And what, exactly, is being mastered?

It matters more than it sounds like it should. Whatever answer you hold, even if you've never put it into words, decides how you treat yourself every single day. Most of the ways people fail at this are really just the result of answering that question badly.

Most of us answer it like a war. There's the real me, the sensible one, the one with standards and plans. And then there's the other part: the lazy part, the weak part, the part that wants the sugar and the scrolling and another twenty minutes in bed. Self-mastery, in this picture, means the real me has to defeat the other one. Break it. Shame it into line. Keep it there with a whip.

If that were how it worked, the person who despises themselves the most would be the most disciplined person alive, and you know that isn't true. People who run their inner life like a drill sergeant don't usually end up free. They end up exhausted. They swing between rigid control and rebellious collapse, and the collapse tends to be worse than whatever they were trying to prevent, because it arrives carrying a fresh load of contempt. Researchers who study how people respond to their own failures have found something that surprises anyone who believes in the whip. The people who meet a failure with something closer to understanding than punishment are more willing to try again, and more willing to work on getting better. The whip doesn't teach discipline. It teaches avoidance. It teaches you to stop looking at the thing you failed at, because looking hurts.

The old thinkers weren't naive about any of this. Plato, in one of his most famous images, describes the soul as a chariot. There's a driver, and there are two horses that want to go in different directions, one disciplined and responsive, the other wild and hungry. Notice what the image does not suggest. It doesn't suggest that the way to win is to get rid of the difficult horse. A chariot with half its power gone doesn't go anywhere. The driver's job is to drive, and driving is a different skill from fighting.

The Stoics used a different vocabulary and arrived somewhere similar. They spoke of the ruling part of the mind, the part that judges what things mean and decides what to do about them. What stands out is how they imagine good rule. Not as conquest. More like the work of a capable governor in a province full of people he can't afford to turn against him. A tyrant rules by fear, and a tyrant's state is always one bad day away from revolt. A good governor understands what each part of the population actually needs, grants what's reasonable, refuses what isn't, and does it so consistently that when he gives an order, people believe he means it.

That last part is worth holding onto. Being believed.

So read the sentence differently. To master yourself doesn't mean to beat yourself. It means to become someone who can lead the entire crowd that lives inside you, the tired part, the frightened part, the ambitious part, the part that desperately wants to be liked, and to lead it well enough that when you say something, all of it takes you seriously.

We'll come back to that, because it turns out to be the real destination. But first we need to find out what is actually under your rule. It's a smaller territory than most people assume. And the smallness, strangely, is where the power comes from.

Almost everyone has heard the opening move of Epictetus. Some things are up to us, and some are not. Your opinions, your choices, your desires and aversions, what you do and what you refuse to do, those are yours. Your body, your reputation, your wealth, other people's decisions, the weather, the economy, the final outcome of nearly anything, those are not. It's been repeated so often that it has gone slightly flat, like a coin that's passed through too many hands.

But something in that division rarely gets noticed, and it matters a great deal for anyone trying to master themselves. The line doesn't run between you and the outside world. It runs through the middle of you.

Seneca makes this uncomfortable point in his writing on anger. He describes a class of reactions that arrive before you've had any say in them. You go pale when you're insulted. You flinch when something falls. Your stomach drops at the edge of a high place, or your face goes hot at something embarrassing. He's clear that these are not choices, and that no amount of philosophy will switch them off. Reason doesn't get a vote. The body has already voted. At best, he says, long practice can soften them.

Consider what that means. Even inside your own skin, there are things that are not up to you. You don't choose the first spike of irritation when someone cuts you off in traffic. You don't choose the sinking feeling when an email from your boss lands in your inbox. You don't choose the wave of craving when a certain smell reaches you at the wrong moment. If self-mastery meant never having those reactions, it would be a promise no human being could keep, and everyone who tried would eventually conclude that they were failing.

The Stoics saw it differently. For them, the first reaction isn't the test. It's the weather. What counts is the next step, the small interval, sometimes a fraction of a second, between the thing that happened to you and the thing you decide to do with it. In that interval, the mind can either agree to what it's been shown, or it can hold back and examine it. They had a technical word for that moment of agreement, which we usually translate as assent. And their whole practical psychology rests on the idea that nothing can push you into action without your assent.

That's a narrow space. But it's the space where a life is actually decided. A person who can't find it lives like a billiard ball, moving only when something hits them, going wherever the last collision sent them. A person who finds it, even occasionally, even for just one reaction a day, has located the exact place where a self can exist.

It's easy to nod along with this and then lose the whole thing the moment real life starts, so let's slow down and watch it happen.

Imagine you've spent a week on a proposal. You send it to a colleague whose opinion matters to you, and a few hours later you get a reply. One word. Noted.

Watch how quickly the machinery starts. First comes the flinch, which isn't yours. A tightening somewhere behind the ribs. Then, almost before you've finished reading, the interpretation arrives. They didn't like it. They think it's weak. They've already mentioned it to someone else. This is the beginning of a pattern, and by next quarter you'll be passed over. All of that happens within a few seconds. And all of it feels like perception. It doesn't feel like a story you're telling. It feels like a fact you've discovered.

Then the afternoon goes. You reread the proposal looking for flaws, and of course you find them, because you're looking. You draft a defensive reply, delete it, draft a breezier one, delete that. You rehearse a conversation in the hallway in which you're devastatingly composed. By five o'clock you've spent three hours in a bitter, tiring argument with a person who said exactly one word, and who may have typed it from a phone in the back of a taxi.

Epictetus packed the whole structure into a sentence that's easy to quote and hard to live. People are disturbed not by things themselves, but by the judgments they form about those things. He isn't saying the one-word reply is pleasant. He's saying that what actually hurt you for the next three hours wasn't the reply. It was everything your mind added to it.

The skill, then, is not to feel nothing. It's to catch the addition. To say, in the quiet part of the mind that still has some authority: a message arrived. It contained one word. Everything else is something I'm contributing. You don't have to argue the story down or force yourself to believe a more flattering one. You only have to notice that it is a story. Once you see that, it loosens, because it was relying on being mistaken for reality.

Most lives aren't ruined by crises. We tend to be ready for those, at least a little. Lives are worn down by afternoons like this one, repeated over thousands of days, each one costing a few hours of attention, a little of our calm, and some of our respect for the people around us. The person who learns to catch even half of those additions hasn't just become calmer. They've gotten a good part of their life back.

There's a second territory that belongs to you, and it's the one most people are quietly losing without noticing.

Marcus Aurelius observed, in the private notebooks we now call the Meditations, that the mind takes on the color of what it habitually thinks about. A mind that returns again and again to grievances gradually becomes a grievance. A mind that returns to appetite becomes appetite. He wasn't offering a pretty metaphor. He was describing how a self gets made. You don't become what you intend. You become what you keep attending to.

The Stoics had a word for the discipline of staying present to your own mind. It was prosoche, which translates roughly as attention. They treated it less like one skill among many and more like the ground floor of the whole building. Without it, nothing else is possible. You can't pause between impression and assent if you aren't there for the impression.

Now consider the conditions under which attention gets exercised today. Rarely has so much ingenuity been aimed at a single human capacity. Entire teams of very intelligent people spend their working lives figuring out how to take your next ten seconds, and then the ten after that. This isn't a reason to panic, and it isn't an excuse either. It's simply a fact about the terrain, and mastery requires honest knowledge of the terrain.

Here's one way to see where you actually stand. The next time you pick up your phone, stop for a moment before you unlock it, and ask what you were reaching for. Not what you plan to do. What you were reaching for. Very often the answer is nothing. There was a flicker of boredom, or a flicker of discomfort in whatever you were doing, and the hand moved before any decision had a chance to form. The checking wasn't chosen. It was a reflex, and a reflex that has been trained into you thousands of times.

Nobody who is checking has decided to check. That's the whole problem, and the whole opportunity. Because mastery of attention doesn't begin with a digital detox or a dramatic gesture. It begins with the tiny, almost embarrassing practice of noticing the reach. Noticing the pull toward the thing, and letting it be there for a few seconds without obeying it. Do that and you find that the urge is smaller than it seemed. It rises, peaks, and passes, the way waves do, and it only ever had the strength you lent it by moving.

There's a quiet consequence in all of this. A mind that can't stay with one task for twenty minutes can't be trusted to stay with a commitment for twenty years. The two abilities are the same ability at different scales. Whatever you rebuild in the small, you quietly rebuild in the large.

Beyond attention lies something deeper, the question of what you want, and what happens when what you want starts running things.

Epictetus, who was born into slavery, spoke about freedom with the kind of precision only someone who has lost it can manage. To him, a person is free when nobody can compel or obstruct them. And the surprising part of his argument was where he located the real chains. He pointed out that if you desire something that someone else controls, you have handed that person the keys to you. The man who wants the favor of the powerful is already their servant. The man who wants something a thief can take is already owned by the thief. It's the wanting itself that carries the leash.

It's a hard idea to take in, because we usually think of our wants as expressions of who we are. But look plainly at your own life. Is there anything you couldn't do without, strictly speaking, but have behaved as if you couldn't? A particular comfort you reach for whenever the day gets heavy? A particular person's approval? A particular image of yourself that has to be defended at some cost? Each one of those is a place where someone or something else holds a lever on your behavior. Not because they're cruel. Simply because you've made yourself dependent.

Seneca, who was one of the wealthiest men in Rome, made a point about money that cuts in an unexpected direction. The poor person, he said, is not the one who has little, it's the one who craves more. A man with ten times what he needs and a permanent hunger for more is poorer, in the sense that matters, than someone with a modest amount who is finished wanting. Poverty, in his view, is a condition of the appetite, not the bank balance.

None of this means wanting nothing. The Stoics weren't asking anyone to live in a bare room, staring at a wall. There's a distinction that does a lot of work here. A want you happen to have is one thing, and a want you would choose to have, if you stepped back and looked at it clearly, is another. Most of us are carrying a surprising number of wants we would never have signed off on. The craving for the next small hit of novelty. The urge to be impressive in front of people we don't particularly respect. The appetite for something that was good the first time and has been merely habitual ever since. Self-mastery in this territory is the slow, unglamorous work of sorting those two groups, and gradually letting the second one fade from lack of attention.

And the want that tends to be the most expensive is the want to be approved of. Marcus Aurelius found it genuinely puzzling, and he wrote about it with something close to amusement. He noticed that every person loves themselves more than anyone else, and yet gives their own opinion of themselves less weight than the opinions of other people. How strange that is. You're the one who knows what you actually did, what you intended, how hard it was. Yet a stranger's raised eyebrow can outvote the entire testimony.

A person who has cut that leash, even partly, becomes oddly difficult to steer. Not in a rebellious way. They simply become capable of doing what seems right and sitting through other people's reactions without being governed by them. In a world where most behavior is shaped by the fear of how it will look, this is not a small kind of freedom.

At this point it would be tempting to conclude that mastery is a kind of heroic inner strength, a person standing firm against waves of temptation through sheer force of character. That picture, appealing as it is, is mostly wrong.

Look at how the people with the most self-control actually live. The intuitive guess is that they must be better at resisting temptation, that they have stronger muscles of refusal. But when researchers looked closely, the picture was close to the opposite. People who score high in self-control report fewer temptations. Fewer moments of struggle. They aren't winning more fights. They're having fewer of them. Their lives have been arranged, usually through unremarkable habits and quiet decisions made in advance, so that the difficult moment rarely arrives.

The Stoics understood this too, and it's one of the places where they're more practical than their reputation suggests. In one of his letters, Seneca describes coming home after a day among crowds, and admits that he returns less steady than he left. More greedy, more ambitious, more careless with other people. He says plainly that spending time among people very different from the person you're trying to become is dangerous, because vices spread the way infections do, easily and without anyone intending it. Then he turns it around and says to seek the company of those who will make you better, and to welcome the people you are able to improve.

That is a strikingly modest view of human strength. It says that you are not an island of pure will. You're an organism, shaped by what you're surrounded by: the people you spend time with, the food in the kitchen, what's on the table next to your bed, which apps sit on the first page of your phone, how many steps lie between you and the thing you're trying to avoid. A person who tries to master themselves while living in a setting designed to undermine them isn't showing courage. They're showing a poor grasp of logistics.

So part of mastering yourself turns out to be remarkably unheroic. It's moving the thing out of the house. It's deciding the night before what you'll do when the hard moment comes, so the deciding doesn't have to happen when you're least capable of it. It's making the good option the easy one and the bad option a little bit annoying. It's admitting that you're someone who can be swayed, and designing around that fact instead of pretending to be someone who can't.

There's a kind of pride that disguises itself as discipline, the pride that insists on standing next to the temptation and winning every time. The wiser version asks a quieter question: how do I arrange things so that I'm rarely asked to be a hero in the first place?

There is, however, another side to this, and the Stoics were careful not to let it go missing. If you arrange your whole life around never being uncomfortable, you aren't mastering yourself either. You're just building a smaller cage with softer walls.

Seneca recommended an odd practice. Every so often, he suggested, set aside a few days in which you live on the plainest food, wear the roughest clothes, and sleep without comforts, and ask yourself during those days whether this is really the condition you were so afraid of. He was writing to a friend who, like him, was comfortable, and the point of the exercise was not to punish the comfortable. It was to take away a fear. A great deal of what keeps people obedient to their circumstances is the dread of losing the cushion. Someone who has quietly practiced living without it, even briefly, holds it differently. They can enjoy it without needing it, which turns out to be a very different relationship.

You can see why this belongs in a conversation about self-mastery. A person who is terrified of discomfort can be steered by anyone who threatens it, including their own impulses. The easiest way for the part of you that wants to avoid effort to win an argument is to remind you that effort is unpleasant. And if you've never practiced being uncomfortable on purpose, you'll find that argument very persuasive.

The practice doesn't need to be dramatic. A cold shower, a skipped dessert, a walk in bad weather, a hard conversation held without the usual cushioning of excuses. Anything, really, that gently tests whether you can tolerate what you've learned to avoid. What matters is the motive. If you're doing it to look tough, or to prove something to an invisible audience, you've swapped one form of dependence for another. If you're doing it to discover that you're more capable than you feared, that the discomfort was smaller than the dread, then each time you've retrieved a little piece of your own freedom.

Comfort isn't the enemy. The Stoics were very clear about that. Needing it is.

All of this can sound a bit cold, so it's worth saying something the caricature of Stoicism gets completely wrong. Mastering yourself does not mean mastering your feelings out of existence.

Seneca, writing to a friend who was grieving, admits that he himself wept at a loss, and then offers a thought that is gentler than most people expect from a Stoic. The eyes shouldn't stay dry when we lose someone we love, he says, but they also shouldn't overflow. We may weep, but we shouldn't wail. Go back over that slowly. It isn't a ban on grief. It's a description of grief that stays inside a person's life instead of taking it over. The tears are allowed. What isn't wise is letting the sorrow become the one making all the decisions.

That distinction runs through everything. There's the person who is angry, and there's the person who acts out of anger, and they're only the same person for a few minutes if you're lucky. The first is human. The second is the one who sends the message they'll spend a week apologizing for.

Seneca wrote an entire work on anger, and its most useful advice is almost laughably simple. Delay. Anger, he points out, needs speed. It burns hottest at the beginning and loses force with every passing minute, so the most powerful remedy is simply time. He even repeats a story about Plato, who, having become furious with a servant, handed the punishment over to someone else, saying he couldn't be the one to deliver it while angry. Whether or not every detail is exactly as it was told, the principle is sound. If you wouldn't trust yourself to decide in this state, don't decide in this state. Wait until the person who's acting is someone you'd be willing to be responsible for.

Fear works the same way, and Seneca had a sharp observation about it. We are, he said, more often frightened than actually hurt. We suffer more in imagination than in reality. Recall the last thing you dreaded for weeks. How much of that dread was spent on a version of the event that never arrived, and how much on the actual event, which turned out to be survivable, shorter, and stranger than you'd pictured?

So mastery of emotion isn't about silence inside. It's about standing in a particular spot relative to the noise. You can feel the anger, name it, let it move through you, and still be the one who chooses what happens next. A person who can do that isn't less alive than someone swept along. They're more alive, if anything, because they get to experience the feeling and then still be there afterward.

Now we can return to the two people at the start of this, the one who makes the promise at night and the one who breaks it at dawn. Everything we've covered leads to a single place, and that place is trust.

Every time you tell yourself you'll do something and then don't, something is recorded. Not dramatically, not with guilt or ceremony, just quietly, the way a ledger records. The part of you that makes the promise is, in effect, writing a check. The part of you that breaks it is declining to honor it. And over time, without ever making a decision about it, the whole inner population learns that your word means very little. It learns that the voice that speaks at eleven at night is not to be taken seriously by the one who has to get up at six.

That is why so many people feel a strange emptiness around their own ambitions. It isn't that they lack desire. They lack credibility with themselves. They say they're going to start, and some part of them has already stopped listening.

If this is true, then self-mastery isn't mainly about intensity. It's about reliability. It's about becoming a person whose commitments carry weight with the one person who knows exactly how many of them were kept.

That changes how you should begin. Epictetus gave a piece of advice about anger that works for almost any habit. If you want to stop being quick-tempered, he said, don't feed it, and keep count. Tell yourself that today you went without losing your temper, and then the next day, and so on, one day at a time. He didn't ask for a transformation. He asked for a tally. And he said, in effect, that the strength of a habit comes from the accumulation of its repetitions, in either direction. Walking is built by walking, reading by reading, and an angry disposition by anger.

So the commitments you make should be almost insultingly small. Five minutes. One page. A single glass of water before the phone. This can feel silly, especially to ambitious people who believe that bigger promises show greater seriousness. But the size of the promise isn't the point. The point is the record. A promise you keep, even a trivial one, is evidence. And evidence is the only thing the other parts of you will accept. You can't argue yourself into trusting yourself. You can only demonstrate it, slowly, in a quiet language of small things done when you said you'd do them.

Do that for weeks and something shifts. The morning voice begins to hesitate before cancelling, because it's no longer sure the night voice was bluffing. And that hesitation, that tiny doubt about whether it should go ahead and give up, is the beginning of rule. Not rule by force. Rule by being believed.

You will, of course, fail. Probably this week. Anyone who tells you that mastery means a flawless record is describing a person who doesn't exist, and teaching you to feel like a fraud whenever you're not that person.

What matters is what happens after. Here Seneca offers one of the most humane practices in all of ancient philosophy. He describes a habit he credits to a philosopher named Sextius. At the end of every day, when the light was out and the house had gone quiet, Seneca would go back over the whole day, examining what he'd said and done. He hid nothing from himself and skipped nothing. And then comes the line I find the most striking. He tells himself not to do that again, and says that this time, he forgives himself.

Look at the structure, because it's subtle. There's an honest accounting. There's a clear instruction for the future. And there's forgiveness, in the same breath, without any ceremony of self-punishment. It's the voice of a good judge who actually wants the person in front of him to improve. Sextius, according to Seneca, asked himself a set of questions at the end of each day. What ailment of mine did I cure today? What fault did I resist? In what way am I better? Notice that these are questions about progress, not perfection. They assume you're a work in progress, which you are.

Compare that with the way most people end their days. Some skip the reckoning altogether, because they suspect it will hurt. Others hold a trial in the dark, prosecuting themselves with every failure from the past decade, and call that self-awareness. Neither one improves anyone. One avoids the information, and the other drowns in it.

A relapse isn't the failure. The failure is the verdict you pass afterward, if the verdict is that you're the kind of person who can't. That conclusion is more damaging than the original lapse, because it turns one bad hour into a permanent identity. The person who has actually learned something about mastery treats a lapse as data. What happened, what led up to it, what can be changed, and then back to the small promises, with no long ceremony in between.

This is what it looks like to govern a province well. When something goes wrong, you don't burn the village. You find out why, fix the cause, and keep the roads open.

There's one more question that tends to get skipped, and the ancient writers would have been uncomfortable with how rarely it's asked. Mastery of yourself, for what?

Discipline by itself is a tool, and tools have no opinions. A person can be extraordinarily disciplined in the service of something small, or cruel, or hollow. Someone can wake at four, never miss a workout, control every expense, and arrange every hour, and still be pointed at nothing in particular, a well-run machine with no destination. Self-control without direction doesn't make a life. It makes a very efficient version of whatever the person already was.

The Stoics refused to separate mastery from character. For them, the point of ruling your impulses was to be able to act well: to be fair when it costs you, to be brave when it's inconvenient, to be honest with people who would prefer otherwise, to keep your head when others are losing theirs. Self-command was the means. Being a decent, useful human being was the end. Marcus Aurelius even wrote that what harms the hive harms the bee, a reminder that no one's private excellence is entirely private. A person who masters themselves and then uses that strength only to pile up advantages for themselves has missed most of the point.

This is also a practical test. When you're deciding whether some discipline is worth building, ask what it frees you to do. Does it make you more available to the people who depend on you? More steady when they're not? More capable of telling the truth, or of finishing something that matters? If the answer is yes, it's the right kind. If the only answer is that it makes you look more impressive, or feel more in control, then it's probably decoration.

The strongest self-mastery tends to look, from the outside, almost dull. A person who is reliably kind. Who does what they said they'd do. Who isn't thrown by a bad day, and doesn't make everyone around them pay for it. There's no spectacle in it. But those are the people others lean on, and being the person others can lean on is one of the oldest meanings of strength.

We should now be a little honest about the second half of the sentence. Master yourself, and you will master your life.

It's a lovely promise, and in the way it's usually understood, it's also false. You can do everything we've talked about, catch your stories, guard your attention, pare down your wants, arrange your surroundings, practice discomfort, keep the small promises, forgive yourself and continue, and life will still do what it does. It will take people from you. It will hand your plans to someone else. It will deliver illness, or money trouble, or a long stretch where nothing works and no one notices how hard you're trying.

Marcus Aurelius is the clearest proof. He wrote a book of private reflections on how to be a person of discipline and fairness, and he spent much of his reign on the frontier of the empire, dealing with war and plague. Many of his children died young. The son who succeeded him is remembered as a disaster. And nothing in those notebooks reads like a man announcing that he's finished. They read like the pages of someone still working at it, reminding himself, scolding himself, steadying himself, again and again. We call them the Meditations, but the title they're often given in the original is more modest. Roughly, it means to himself.

To himself. Which brings us back to the strange fact at the beginning, that there are two parties in one person. Here was a man who, by any outward measure, was among the most powerful human beings alive, and what he had was a notebook in which one part of him spoke to another.

So what does the second half of the sentence actually promise? Not control over events. Something quieter. That what happens to you will no longer be able to decide who you are. That you'll meet the next loss, or the next injustice, or the next ordinary Tuesday, as someone who still has access to their own judgment, rather than as someone who has been taken over by the situation. You won't be the master of your life the way a king is master of a kingdom. You'll be the master of your response, which is the only place anyone has ever truly had authority.

And that turns out to be most of what a life is. Not the sequence of things that happen, but the way each one is met. If you can change how you meet things, you have changed the substance of the life, even when the facts stay exactly the same.

So here is where the sentence leaves us.

There isn't a master and a servant after all. That was a useful way to begin, but it was only a first approximation. What there is, is a crowd of impulses and fears and wants and memories, all of which have been around much longer than your intentions, and one slender part of you that can step back, look at what's happening, and choose. Mastery is the slow process of that part earning the trust of the rest. Not by shouting, not by punishment, but by being honest, being consistent, and being modest enough in its demands that it can keep its word.

Tonight, around eleven, you'll probably make a promise again. Make it a small one. Make it one the person at six o'clock can keep without heroics. And when that person wakes up and begins the usual arithmetic, don't fight. Just do the small thing, and let it be recorded.

Over time, the two of you stop sounding so different. The one who decides at night and the one who has to carry it out in the morning begin to speak in the same voice. And at some point, without any announcement, you'll notice that there's only one of you left, making the plans and keeping them. That is what the sentence was pointing at all along.
